topics: 🍎 Testing 'Constant Tears' — a cascade of unresolved dilemmas about how to feed the fig-bulk
⏪ Retroactive or From Now? — Pinḥas's question about when a confirmed blemish takes effect
🦷 Nose, Lip, and Teeth — new blemishes, and which teeth are 'hidden' and don't count
🫘 A Missing Internal Organ — does a lack that isn't visible from outside disqualify an offering?
🐑 Tail and Genitalia — the mishna's list, and a three-way dispute over damaged testicles

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Feeding Tests to Hidden Blemishes
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 39a–39b
overview.hebrewSource: חוּטִין הַחִיצוֹנוֹת שֶׁנִּפְגְּמוּ, וְשֶׁנִּגְמְמוּ, הַפְּנִימִיִּם שֶׁנֶּעֶקְרוּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by piling up unresolved procedural questions about the fig-bulk fodder test for 'constant tears' — before or after eating, tied or free, in the field or the city — each left as a standing dilemma. A practical question follows: if the animal is only confirmed blemished after the three-month test, does that blemish apply retroactively? New mishnayot then add blemishes of the nose, lip, and teeth (external gums count, but the hidden inner teeth do not), before the Gemara opens a much larger question: does a defect in an internal organ, invisible from outside, count as a disqualifying 'lack' at all? The daf closes with the mishna's list of tail and genital blemishes, including a three-way dispute over damaged testicles.

slides.title: 🍎 Testing the Fig-Bulk: An Unresolved Cascade
slides.subtitle: The Gemara piles up procedural questions about the moist/dry fodder test — and answers none of them

steps.content: 1️⃣ Fed only at the first meal, or at every meal? Before eating (clearly effective, like medicine) or after eating?
2️⃣ Before drinking (clearly effective, like barley) or after drinking?
3️⃣ While tied up, or untied (clearly effective, since the animal is at ease)? Alone, or with a companion animal?
4️⃣ In the city, or in the field (clearly effective, since the animal is calm)? Rav Ashi adds: what about a garden just outside the city?

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Every one of these questions is left standing — תֵּיקוּ — the Gemara supplies no resolution.

slides.title: ⏪ Does the Blemish Apply Retroactively?
slides.hebrewSource: אֲכַל וְלָא אִיתַּסִּי — לְמַפְרֵעַ הָוֵי מוּמָא, אוֹ מִיכָּן וּלְהַבָּא הָוֵי מוּמָא
slides.label: Pinḥas's question to Shmuel:
slides.text: If the animal ate the fodder as required and was not healed, is the blemish considered to have existed retroactively from the start, or only from the moment it is confirmed? The practical difference: if the animal was redeemed during the three-month test and someone used the redemption money, did he misuse consecrated property? Shmuel had no answer, remarking wryly, quoting Isaiah 33:23, ״פִּסְחִים בָּזְזוּ בַז״ — 'the lame take the prey,' since even his unlearned brother could ask a question he could not answer.

slides.title: 🦷 New Mishna: Nose, Lip, and Teeth
slides.subtitle: Some blemishes count only if visible from outside
rows: If nostrils are pierced into each other: visible from outside = blemish; visible only inside = not a blemish
Outer lip pierced, damaged, or split
Rav Pappa: refers specifically to the protruding outer row of the lip
Does NOT count (R' Ḥanina ben Antigonus)
Hidden location; R' Yehoshua ben Kefutzai: still disqualifies from the altar, just doesn't permit outside slaughter

callout.label: Underlying test:
callout.text: Throughout this sugya, whether a blemish is exposed (גָּלוּי) or hidden determines whether it permits slaughtering the firstborn outside the Temple.

slides.title: 🫘 Does a Missing Internal Organ Count as a 'Lack'?
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot on kidneys seem to contradict — how many tannaim are really disputing, and about what?

lines.speaker: Baraita 1
lines.text: "The two kidneys" (Leviticus 3:4) excludes an animal with only one kidney, or with three, from the altar.

lines.speaker: Baraita 2
lines.text: But the singular "he shall take it away" comes to INCLUDE an animal with one kidney as fit!

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef
lines.text: No dispute at all — both agree an internal lack disqualifies. One baraita means it was BORN with two and lost one (disqualified); the other means it was born with only one from the start (naturally whole, so fit).

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yoḥanan
lines.text: No dispute either — but the real variable is TIMING: lacking a kidney before slaughter disqualifies; lacking one only after the blood is collected does not, since the verse's requirements apply only up through the blood's collection.

callout.label: Rava's addendum:
callout.text: Since an offering can shift from 'in its first year' to 'in its second year' between slaughter and blood-collection, 'hours disqualify' sacrificial animals — timing is measured precisely.

slides.title: 🐑 New Mishna: Tail and Genital Blemishes
slides.subtitle: The mishna's list, plus a three-way dispute over damaged testicles (Leviticus 22:24)

boxes.title: The Mishna's List
items: Damaged genital pouch (but NOT if entirely removed, and NOT the organ itself — R' Elazar)
Tail damaged from the tailbone (not from a joint, which heals)
Exposed tailbone, or a full fingerbreadth of flesh missing between vertebrae

boxes.title: R' Yehuda: All in the Testicles
items: Bruised, crushed, torn, or cut testicles are all blemishes — they visibly shrink or hang loosely

boxes.title: R' Elazar b. Yaakov / R' Yosei
items: R' Elazar b. Yaakov: all four terms apply only to the penis, not the testicles
R' Yosei: bruised/crushed testicles ARE a blemish (they're simply gone); torn/cut testicles are NOT (they're still physically present)

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam even reports a case where a wolf tore off an animal's genital pouch and it grew back — showing regeneration can undercut a blemish claim.

summary.principle: Beyond the many unresolved procedural questions about testing a blemish, the daf's core theme is visibility and timing: a blemish must generally be exposed rather than hidden, and its status can hinge on exactly when — before or after slaughter, before or after blood collection — it is found.

flowSteps.content: 🍎 Numerous procedural details of the fodder test are left unresolved (תֵּיקוּ)
⏪ Whether a confirmed blemish counts retroactively remains an open question
🦷 Nose, lip, and outer teeth blemishes count; hidden inner ('double') teeth generally do not

columns.content: 🫘 A missing internal organ can disqualify — but timing and "born that way" both matter
🐑 Tail, genital, and testicle blemishes are each defined by visibility and manner of damage

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: exposure and precise timing consistently determine whether a physical defect counts as a disqualifying blemish

quiz.q: What is the Gemara's ultimate conclusion about the many procedural questions raised concerning the fig-bulk fodder test (before/after eating, tied/untied, city/field)?
o: All are resolved leniently
All are resolved strictly
They are left unresolved (teiku)
Only the city/field question is resolved
quiz.e: Each of these dilemmas is explicitly left standing with no resolution, marked teiku.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference Pinḥas raises regarding whether a confirmed blemish (after the 3-month tear test) applies retroactively?
o: Whether the animal may be eaten at all
Whether redemption money used before the blemish was confirmed constitutes misuse of consecrated property (me'ila)
Whether the animal must be examined by three witnesses
Whether the priest may eat the meat
quiz.e: If the blemish is retroactive, using the redemption money before confirmation would be considered misuse of still-consecrated property; if not, no misuse occurred.

quiz.q: According to the mishna's ruling (as explained by Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus), why don't the internal 'double teeth' count as a disqualifying blemish for outside slaughter?
o: Because teeth are never considered blemishes
Because their location is hidden/internal, and a blemish generally must be exposed to permit slaughtering the firstborn outside the Temple
Because only the nose and lip can be blemished
Because double teeth cannot be damaged
quiz.e: The recurring principle in this sugya is that a disqualifying blemish for outside slaughter must be visible/exposed; the double teeth are hidden and therefore excluded.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan resolve the apparent contradiction between two baraitot about an animal missing a kidney?
o: He says the baraitot cannot be reconciled
The dispute is about timing: lacking a kidney before slaughter disqualifies the offering, but lacking one only after the blood is already collected does not
He rules that a missing kidney is never a disqualification
He says both baraitot are talking about the same case
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that everyone agrees an internal lack disqualifies, but the difference is timing: the requirement of wholeness applies only up through the collection of the blood, not afterward.

quiz.q: In the three-way dispute over damaged testicles (bruised, crushed, torn, or cut), what does Rabbi Yosei hold?
o: All four terms apply only to the penis
All four terms apply only to the testicles equally
Bruised/crushed testicles are a blemish since they are effectively gone, but torn/cut testicles are not, since they remain physically present
None of the four terms ever create a blemish
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei distinguishes based on whether the testicle still physically exists: bruised or crushed means it is essentially destroyed (a blemish), while torn or cut means it is still present, just detached (not a blemish by his reasoning).
